opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that it *is* a hypothesis. OpenAI hasn't told us how o1 works, so anyone outside the company, including me, is doing a kind of reverse engineering from the outside. I try to be honest about that. What I can do is reason from what we know about these systems in general, from the limited hints they've given, and from how the model actually behaves when you test it.

My best guess is that they've gone beyond plain autoregressive generation. They take a base LLM and do something like reinforcement learning over generated chains of thought. The model produces many candidate reasoning traces, some signal tells you which ones led to correct answers, and that feedback shapes what the model generates. Then at inference time you're spending more compute, generating and evaluating longer internal "thinking" before you commit to an answer. Conceptually it's closer to AlphaGo-style ideas, learning which moves to make in a space of reasoning steps, than to just predicting the next token from web text.

How confident am I? I'd separate it into layers. I'm fairly confident about the broad strokes: post-training with RL on reasoning traces, plus extra inference-time computation. The behavior is consistent with that. On our planning benchmarks, things like Blocksworld and especially the obfuscated "Mystery Blocksworld" versions, o1 does substantially better than the standard LLMs, which had essentially collapsed there. That's a qualitative shift, and pure scaling of the same old autoregressive approach doesn't easily explain it. Also, latency and cost go up with problem difficulty, which tells you it's doing variable amounts of work per query.

I'm much less certain about the specifics. Is there an explicit search procedure at inference time, or has the search been compiled into the model during training? What exactly is the reward signal, and how much comes from verifiable domains like math and code? Is there one model or several pieces? Those details matter, and I don't think anyone outside can claim to know.

The thing I keep emphasizing is that the uncertainty about the mechanism shouldn't turn into uncertainty about the evaluation. Whatever is going on inside, we can still test it. And what we see is that it's better, but it's not giving guarantees. It still makes mistakes on longer problems, it sometimes says an unsolvable problem is solvable, and it costs a lot more per query. So my position is: I'm humble about *how* it works, I'm reasonably firm about *what* it does and doesn't do, and I think it's a different kind of system than the LLMs I was critiquing before. I'd call it a large reasoning model, not just a language model. That's why I've been careful to update my views on it rather than just repeat what I said about GPT-4.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me be clear up front: I don't know how O1 works, and neither does anyone outside OpenAI. That's the first thing. What I have is a hypothesis, and I try to be honest that it's a hypothesis.

The way I'd frame it is this. We know some things from what OpenAI has said publicly. We know there's a reinforcement learning stage on top of the base model. We know it generates these long chains of so-called reasoning tokens before it answers, and that inference time scales with the difficulty of the problem. Those are the constraints any explanation has to satisfy.

My guess, and it is a guess, is that it's something like an approximate retrieval over reasoning traces. During training, you generate many candidate chains of thought, you have some verifier or reward signal that tells you which ones lead to correct answers, and you use RL to shift the distribution toward the productive ones. At inference time, the model is essentially sampling in that learned space, maybe with some search on top, maybe not. I lean toward thinking there isn't an elaborate explicit search procedure like MCTS at test time, but I hold that loosely. It would not shock me to be wrong about that.

Where I feel more confident is at the level of what kind of thing it is, rather than the mechanism. Whatever O1 is doing, it's still an LLM producing tokens. It's not a system with an internal world model that it's provably checking against. That's why I keep saying it's "approximate reasoning" or, as I've put it before, it's moved from approximate retrieval to approximate reasoning. The failure modes we see, where it's confidently wrong on problems that are slight variations of ones it handles fine, are consistent with that picture. If I saw a system whose errors behaved like a sound planner's errors, I'd have to update.

So how do I assess the uncertainty? I'd put it this way. On the mechanism, high uncertainty. On the broad characterization, moderate confidence, and importantly it's falsifiable. We ran the planning benchmarks, PlanBench, the Blocksworld and the obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld variants, and O1 did markedly better than GPT-4 class models, which is real and I said so. But performance still drops off as plan length grows, and it still degrades on the obfuscated versions in a way a real planner wouldn't. Those results are what I'm anchoring to. If someone releases evidence showing an explicit verifier in the loop at inference, or if the scaling behavior changes qualitatively, I'll revise.

The thing I'd caution against is the opposite error, which is treating the lack of disclosure as license to believe whatever is most flattering to the system. Not knowing cuts both ways. The burden should be on empirical testing, not on speculation in either direction, and I try to keep my own claims tethered to the experiments we can actually run.

Until we have that evidence, I think we should be quite explicit about the uncertainty.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate what we can observe from the explanation we give for it. We can observe that giving the system more time at inference appears to improve its performance on certain tasks. But that doesn’t uniquely tell us what mechanism is operating underneath. It could involve generating and evaluating intermediate solutions, some form of search, or a combination of techniques.

So my hypothesis is just that—a hypothesis. I don’t have access to OpenAI’s internal implementation. The useful question is whether it makes predictions that distinguish it from other explanations. Until we have that evidence, we should keep several possibilities open.
